Hypothesis Tests

Source: vignettes/articles/htest.qmd 
library(dplyr)
library(apa7)
apa7_defaults(font_family = "Open Sans", line_spacing = 1.5)

The apa_htest function runs common hypothesis tests on the variables in a data frame and makes an APA-style table with one row per test. Each row has descriptive statistics, the test statistic and its degrees of freedom, the p-value, and an effect size with its confidence interval. The tests come from the stats package (e.g., t.test), and the effect sizes are computed from the data by the effectsize package.

Test test Formula Default effect size
Welch’s or Student’s t test "t" y ~ group Cohen’s d
One-sample t test "t" y ~ 1 Cohen’s d
Paired t test "t" Pair(pre, post) ~ 1 dav
Wilcoxon rank-sum test "wilcoxon" y ~ group Rank-biserial r
Wilcoxon signed-rank test "wilcoxon" y ~ 1 or Pair(pre, post) ~ 1 Rank-biserial r
Correlation test "cor" y ~ x The correlation itself
Chi-square test of independence "chisq" y ~ group Cramér’s V

Several outcomes on the left side of the formula, joined with +, give one row each. Test results that were already computed (e.g., by t.test) can also be formatted (see Test Results Already Computed). In the console, apa_htest returns an ordinary tibble. In Quarto and R Markdown documents, the tibble is displayed as an APA-style table automatically, and apa_flextable customizes it further.

Comparing Two Groups

Welch’s t test

The sat.act data in the psych package (Revelle, 2026) has self-reported ACT and SAT scores from 700 people. Do men and women differ in their scores? The grouping variable must have exactly two values. Make it a factor with readable labels, and give the test scores names that read well in a table.

d_sat <- psych::sat.act |>
  as_tibble() |>
  mutate(
    Gender = factor(gender, levels = 1:2, labels = c("Men", "Women")),
    ACT,
    `SAT-V` = SATV,
    `SAT-Q` = SATQ
  )
apa_htest(
  d_sat,
  ACT + `SAT-V` + `SAT-Q` ~ Gender
) |> 
  mutate(`*df*` = as.integer(`*df*`)) |> 
  apa_flextable()

By default, the table shows each group’s mean (M) and standard deviation (SD) under a spanner with the group’s name. Then come Welch’s t test, its p-value, and Cohen’s d with its 95% confidence interval. Welch’s test does not assume equal variances, so its degrees of freedom are not whole numbers and differ from row to row. They get their own column (df). When all rows have the same degrees of freedom, as in Student’s t test below, they appear in the column header instead (e.g., t(698)).

Differences are the first group (in factor level order) minus the second, so a positive d means that men have the larger mean. To flip the direction, reorder the factor levels (e.g., with forcats::fct_rev).

Student’s t test and Hedges’ g

With var_equal = TRUE, the table shows Student’s t test, which assumes equal variances, and Cohen’s d uses the pooled standard deviation. Hedges’ g corrects d for its small-sample bias.

apa_htest(
  d_sat,
  ACT + `SAT-V` ~ Gender,
  var_equal = TRUE,
  effect_size = "hedges_g"
)

One-sided tests and other test options

Other arguments are passed to the test function. For example, alternative = "greater" makes a one-sided test, here of whether men have higher SAT Quantitative scores than women. Effect size intervals stay two-sided, and the table note says that the p-values are one-sided.

tbl_greater <- apa_htest(
  d_sat,
  `SAT-Q` ~ Gender,
  alternative = "greater"
)
tbl_greater
apa_note(tbl_greater)
[1] "Welch's *t* test compares the groups of Gender without assuming equal variances. The *p*-value is one-sided (alternative: greater). Cohen's *d* uses the average of the two groups' variances. CI = confidence interval for Cohen's *d*."

One-Sample Tests

To compare a mean with a fixed value, put 1 on the right side of the formula and give the value as mu. SAT section scores were scaled to have a mean of 500. Is the mean SAT Verbal score in sat.act different from 500?

apa_htest(d_sat, `SAT-V` ~ 1, mu = 500)

Paired Tests

One pair

In the sleep data, 10 patients each took two sleep drugs. Paired data must be in wide format, with one column per measurement. Put the two variables of each pair in Pair(), with 1 on the right side of the formula, as in t.test:

d_sleep <- sleep |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = group, values_from = extra, names_prefix = "Drug ")
d_sleep
# A tibble: 10 × 3
   ID    `Drug 1` `Drug 2`
   <fct>    <dbl>    <dbl>
 1 1          0.7      1.9
 2 2         -1.6      0.8
 3 3         -0.2      1.1
 4 4         -1.2      0.1
 5 5         -0.1     -0.1
 6 6          3.4      4.4
 7 7          3.7      5.5
 8 8          0.8      1.6
 9 9          0        4.6
10 10         2        3.4
tbl_sleep <- apa_htest(d_sleep, Pair(`Drug 1`, `Drug 2`) ~ 1)

The table note extracted with apa_note says how d was standardized:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-paired
#| tbl-cap: "Paired-Samples *t* test"
#| apa-note: !expr 'apa7::apa_note(tbl_sleep)'
tbl_sleep
```
Note. Paired t test compares Drug 1 with Drug 2. dav divides the mean difference by the average of the two variables’ standard deviations (Lakens, 2013). CI = confidence interval for dav.

With one pair, the variable names head their descriptive statistics, and differences are the first variable minus the second.

Effect sizes for paired data

Paired data have several versions of Cohen’s d, which differ in the standard deviation that the mean difference is divided by (Lakens, 2013):

effect_size Effect size Mean difference divided by
"d_av" (default) dav The average of the two variables’ SDs
"d_z" dz The SD of the differences
"d_rm" drm The SD of the differences, corrected for the correlation between the variables
"g_av", "g_z", "g_rm" gav, gz, grm As above, with Hedges’ small-sample correction

The default, dav, is on the same scale as d for two independent groups, so it can be compared with between-subjects studies. dz is often much larger, because the SD of the differences is small when the two variables are highly correlated. It describes how consistent the change is rather than how large it is relative to individual differences. "cohens_d" is the same as "d_av", and "hedges_g" is the same as "g_av". All of them come from effectsize::repeated_measures_d.

apa_htest(d_sleep, Pair(`Drug 1`, `Drug 2`) ~ 1, effect_size = "d_z")

Several pairs

Join several pairs with + to get one row per pair. Their descriptive statistics are headed “First” and “Second” unless you set pair_labels. In this made-up study, anxiety and depression were measured before and after an intervention:

set.seed(1)
d_prepost <- tibble(
  `Anxiety Pre` = rnorm(40, 50, 10),
  `Anxiety Post` = `Anxiety Pre` - rnorm(40, 4, 6),
  `Depression Pre` = rnorm(40, 50, 10),
  `Depression Post` = `Depression Pre` - rnorm(40, 1, 6)
)

apa_htest(
  d_prepost,
  Pair(`Anxiety Pre`, `Anxiety Post`) + Pair(`Depression Pre`, `Depression Post`) ~ 1,
  pair_labels = c("Pretest", "Posttest")
) |> 
  mutate(Variable = apa7::hanging_indent(Variable, width = 20)) |> 
  apa_flextable(no_format_columns = Variable) |> 
  flextable::width(width = c(1.58,.5,.5, .02,.5,.5, rep(.6, 3), 1.1))

Each pair uses the rows in which both of its variables are observed.

Wilcoxon Tests

With test = "wilcoxon", the table shows each group’s median (Mdn), the Wilcoxon test statistic (W for the rank-sum test, V for the signed-rank test), and the rank-biserial correlation (rrb). Like other correlations, rrb ranges from −1 to 1 and has no leading zero.

apa_htest(
  d_sat,
  `SAT-V` + `SAT-Q` ~ Gender,
  test = "wilcoxon",
  exact = FALSE
) |> 
  rename(`*Mdn*_Men` = `Men_*Mdn*`,
         `*Mdn*_Women` = `Women_*Mdn*`)

With ties in the data, wilcox.test cannot compute exact p-values and warns about it. exact = FALSE asks for the normal approximation without the warning.

Signed-rank tests use the same formulas as one-sample and paired t tests:

apa_htest(
  d_sleep,
  Pair(`Drug 1`, `Drug 2`) ~ 1,
  test = "wilcoxon",
  exact = FALSE
) |> 
  rename(`*Mdn*_Drug 1` = `Drug 1_*Mdn*`,
         `*Mdn*_Drug 2` = `Drug 2_*Mdn*`)

Every patient slept more with Drug 2 (or the same with both), so rrb is −1.00.

Correlation Tests

With test = "cor", each variable on the left is correlated with the variable on the right. The table shows the sample size, the correlation with its confidence interval, and the t test of the correlation. The epi.bfi data in the psychTools package (Revelle, 2019) has personality, depression, and anxiety scores from 231 undergraduates. How strongly do depression, anxiety, and extraversion correlate with neuroticism?

d_personality <- psychTools::epi.bfi |>
  as_tibble() |>
  select(
    Neuroticism = bfneur,
    Extraversion = bfext,
    Depression = bdi,
    Anxiety = traitanx
  )

apa_htest(
  d_personality,
  Depression + Anxiety + Extraversion ~ Neuroticism,
  test = "cor"
)

method = "spearman" or method = "kendall" gives rank correlations, which have no confidence interval:

apa_htest(
  d_personality,
  Depression + Anxiety ~ Neuroticism,
  test = "cor",
  method = "spearman",
  exact = FALSE
)

To display all the correlations among a set of variables, use apa_cor (see the correlations article).

Chi-Square Tests of Independence

With test = "chisq", each variable on the left is cross-tabulated with the variable on the right and tested for independence. The default effect size is Cramér’s V. For 2 × 2 tables, effect_size = "phi" gives φ.

The survey data in the MASS package (Venables & Ripley, 2002) has the answers of 237 statistics students to questions about themselves. Do women and men differ in how often they exercise or in which hand they write with?

d_survey <- MASS::survey |>
  as_tibble() |>
  transmute(
    Sex,
    Exercise = factor(Exer, levels = c("None", "Some", "Freq"),
                      labels = c("None", "Some", "Frequent")),
    `Writing Hand` = W.Hnd
  )

tbl_chisq <- apa_htest(d_survey, Exercise + `Writing Hand` ~ Sex, test = "chisq")
```{r}
#| label: tbl-chisq
#| tbl-cap: Chi-Square Tests of Exercise and Writing Hand by Sex
#| apa-note: !expr 'apa7::apa_note(tbl_chisq)'
tbl_chisq
```
Note. Chi-square tests of independence with Sex. 2 × 2 tables use Yates’s continuity correction. CI=confidence interval for Cramér’s V.

As in chisq.test, 2 × 2 tables (here, Writing Hand × Sex) use Yates’s continuity correction, and the note says so. Use correct = FALSE to turn it off. If some expected counts are small, chisq.test warns that the chi-square approximation may be incorrect. To display the cell counts of one contingency table, use apa_chisq (see the contingency tables article).

Customizing Hypothesis Test Tables

Notes

apa_htest records how the tests were done, and apa_note turns that record into note text. The note names the test, explains the effect size and the abbreviations, and, when used, explains stars and bold values. The text is in markdown, and it does not start with “Note.” because apaquarto adds that.

tbl_sat <- apa_htest(
  d_sat,
  `SAT-V` + `SAT-Q` ~ Gender,
  starred = "t"
)
apa_note(tbl_sat)
[1] "Welch's *t* tests compare the groups of Gender without assuming equal variances. Cohen's *d* uses the average of the two groups' variances. CI = confidence interval for Cohen's *d*. ^\\* ^*p* ≤ .05. ^\\*\\* ^*p* ≤ .01. ^\\*\\*\\* ^*p* ≤ .001."

With apaquarto, use apa_note in the apa-note chunk option with !expr. Chunk options are evaluated before the chunk runs, so make the table in an earlier chunk (as tbl_sat was made above) and display it in the chunk with the note:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-sat-note
#| apa7-width: landscape
#| column: page-right
#| tbl-cap: Welch's *t* Tests Comparing SAT Scores of Men and Women
#| apa-note: !expr apa7::apa_note(tbl_sat)
tbl_sat
```
Note. Welch’s t tests compare the groups of Gender without assuming equal variances. Cohen’s d uses the average of the two groups’ variances. CI = confidence interval for Cohen’s d. * p ≤ .05. ** p ≤ .01. *** p ≤ .001.

Without apaquarto, apa_flextable(tbl, note = TRUE) puts the same note below the table. Do not combine it with the apa-note chunk option, or the note will appear twice.

apa_flextable(tbl_sat, note = TRUE)

The generated note is a starting point. With collapse = NULL, apa_note returns one sentence per element, so you can drop, reword, or add sentences.

Stars and bold values

starred puts significance stars on the columns you name, and bolded bolds significant values:

apa_htest(
  d_sat,
  `SAT-V` + `SAT-Q` ~ Gender,
  bolded = "p"
)

Fewer columns

descriptives = FALSE drops the descriptive statistics, and effect_size = "none" drops the effect size:

apa_htest(
  d_sat,
  `SAT-V` + `SAT-Q` ~ Gender,
  descriptives = FALSE,
  effect_size = "none"
)

Labels

Variable names are converted to title case (e.g., bdi becomes Bdi). For better labels, rename the variables before calling apa_htest, as was done throughout this article. Because the output is a tibble, you can also change the labels afterward.

Missing data

Each test uses the rows in which the outcome and the grouping (or predictor) variable are observed, so rows can have different sample sizes. In sat.act, for example, 13 people did not report an SAT Quantitative score, so the SAT Quantitative tests above use fewer people than the ACT and SAT Verbal tests. Paired tests use the rows in which both variables of the pair are observed.

Test Results Already Computed

Functions like t.test return htest objects, which have the test statistic and p-value but not the data. apa_htest also accepts these objects, or a list of objects of the same kind, with one row per test. The names of the list label the rows:

neuroticism_tests <- list(
  Depression = cor.test(d_personality$Neuroticism, d_personality$Depression),
  Anxiety = cor.test(d_personality$Neuroticism, d_personality$Anxiety),
  Extraversion = cor.test(d_personality$Neuroticism, d_personality$Extraversion)
)
apa_htest(neuroticism_tests) |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)

Effect sizes, however, are computed from what the objects keep, and that is not always enough:

Test Effect size from the object
One-sample t test Cohen’s d = t/√n, exactly
Paired t test dz = t/√n, exactly (not dav, which needs the data)
Welch’s or Student’s t test Cohen’s d ≈ 2t/√df, which assumes groups of equal size
Correlation test The correlation itself
Chi-square test of independence Cramér’s V (or φ, or Cohen’s w), exactly, from the observed table
Wilcoxon tests None, because the group sizes are not kept

For two groups, the approximation can be noticeably off when the groups differ in size or variance, as men (247) and women (453) do in sat.act. The note says that it is an approximation:

t.test(`SAT-Q` ~ Gender, data = d_sat) |>
  apa_htest() |>
  apa_flextable(note = TRUE)

When the data are at hand, giving them to apa_htest is better: the effect sizes are then computed from the data rather than approximated from the test statistic, and the table has descriptive statistics.

References

Lakens, D. (2013). Calculating and reporting effect sizes to facilitate cumulative science: A practical primer for t-tests and ANOVAs. Frontiers in Psychology, 4, Article 863. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2013.00863
Revelle, W. (2019). psychTools: Tools to accompany the psych package for psychological research (Version 2.6.4) [Computer software]. Comprehensive R Archive Network. https://doi.org/10.32614/CRAN.package.psychTools
Revelle, W. (2026). psych: Procedures for psychological, psychometric, and personality research (Version 2.6.9) [Computer software]. Northwestern University. https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=psych
Venables, W. N., & Ripley, B. D. (2002). Modern applied statistics with S (4th ed.). Springer. https://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/pub/MASS4/
